utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If I could take you back, Mr. Djordjevic, to the 21st of July, 1998. You said you attended a meeting in Belgrade at President Milosevic's office or at -- somewhere that he kept meetings, and Mr. General Pavkovic presented a plan at that meeting. Did you see whether or not he had a written plan, apart from the map which you saw?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw the map clearly as well as the papers that he relied on while speaking. Now, whether that was a plan or not, I don't know. I sat across from him, several metres away from him, so I couldn't really see what papers he was relying on to give his report.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know if anyone in the MUP obtained a copy or copies of the five-phase plan?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally never saw that plan, nor do I know that any of the attendees at that meeting had a copy of that plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'd like to show you a couple of documents. They're not -- well, you could look at them and I'd just like to have your comment on one or two things.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we have P1226, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is a letter from General Pavkovic, then the head of the Pristina Corps, the commander of the Pristina Corps, to the 3rd Army commander. And here he refers to what the plan envisages, if you look at the second sentence on the main body of the document. Were these areas the -- included in the unblocking operations that were contemplated in the plan or that you heard him speaking about at the meeting in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that occasion he spoke in general terms about basic activities that were to be implemented down there, and the first and most important task at that point in time was unblocking this main road that we have already mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The Pristina-Pec road?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Pristina-Pec-Komorane-Kijevo-Klina, that's one road, and then the other road was from Pristina via Stimlje to Suva Reka and then on to Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we move on to 1227.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And this was phase one, phase two of the five-phase plan he's referring to here? We -- just orient yourself quickly. This is another, without going to the next page, it's another dispatch from General Pavkovic to the third commander -- to the 3rd Army commander. And just focus, if you can, on the first sentence of the document which refers to implementing or implementation of the second stage of the plan and then to item 2. I think in your last answer this is what you referred to, the unblocking of the Dulje-Suva Reka-Stimlje road.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And your question is?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: These were the -- you are familiar with these areas? These were the plans that were contemplated by -- or -- by General Pavkovic --

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you see in item 3 -- and if you see in item 3, as in the previous document, he refers to this global plan as being the outcome of the order of President Milosevic, the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not how it was. The plan stemmed from the order of the Supreme Defence Council, which had a session some ten days prior to that. And the plan envisaged anti-terrorist activities in Kosovo in several phases. Here you can see quite clearly that the commander of the Pristina Corps requests from the army commander permission to act in accordance with the global plan that had already been adopted, to develop it further, and to envisage the forces and the area where there would be further activities. So this has to do with the development of lower-level documents stemming from the plan. So the commander of the Pristina Corps asked for permission from the army commander, and upon receiving that permission these lower-level documents would be further developed concerning specific actions to be undertaken in a specific area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. What I really wanted to focus on is -- without going back to the previous document, I'll just read the part that I referred to. He said at the meeting of the president of the FRY held at his office on the 21st of July, 1998, an order was given to implement the plan for combatting terrorist forces. And in this document which you have, you see -- where are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If you could go back, please, to the first page of this document, item 3 -- oh, item 3 in B/C/S is on the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If you read item 3 in English you see it says that: "This engagement of the most minimal force of the PrK," that's the Pristina Corps, "ensures good support of the MUP units and the energetic and quick conduct of tasks in the spirit of the order of the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia." All I'm asking here -- you know, you see that he is referring in these two documents to the same plans that you discussed the previous day, of unblocking these roads. Didn't the order come from President Milosevic to proceed? This is what Pavkovic seems to be saying -- or General Pavkovic seems to be saying in these two documents.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in all of these documents that we are looking at now, in Pavkovic's letter and in addressing the commander of his 3rd Army, it clearly says that pursuant to the general plan adopted by the president of the FRY, that plan needs to be implemented now. And he asks his commander for a permission to make that plan operational; that is to say, to develop further lower-level documents based on which that plan can be implemented. So it's not contentious at all that they're working pursuant to this general plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I just wanted to know if seeing these two documents from General Pavkovic, if you agree or you're aware that President Milosevic ordered that you officials in Kosovo proceed with the plan. In both of the documents General Pavkovic refers to the order of President Milosevic to proceed. Is that your awareness, that he ordered you to proceed?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That who ordered that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: General Milosevic -- sorry, the FRY President Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you this: In Milosevic's office the global plan was adopted, and at that point in time it was said, "Now it's up to you to start implementing this." This was all that was said in Milosevic's office. And based on that plan there were all these activities within the corps, in the 3rd Army, and with police forces. So it wasn't like Milosevic issued specific tasks during certain phases, no. At that point in time the plan was adopted and it was said that police and military forces would be tasked with working together in order to combat terrorist activities in Kosovo and in accordance with the plan that had been adopted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Now, since I can't get an answer, can I put it this way: Did President Milosevic adopt the plan and was he the person who said, "Now it is up to you to start implementing this"?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it was. The plan was definitely adopted by him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you at that meeting hear him or anyone make reference to the setting up of a Joint Command involving political representatives along with the senior leadership of the MUP and the VJ?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Neither from him nor from anybody else at that meeting did I hear that some Joint Command would be set up, nor did I hear anything concerning any Joint Command. All that was said was that this plan would have to be implemented together by army and MUP forces and that certain politicians would be visiting the area with their tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we have a look at P1245, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is a document from the Federal Ministry of Justice of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia of the 12th of July, 2002, and it is in response to some questions put to it by the representatives of this Tribunal. And in the first bullet point you'll see that they say: "The Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija was formed on the order by the FRY President in June 1998 without any specific document." Do you have any reason to contest the truth of this statement? Can you say that this is not true, that he formed the Joint Command in June 1998?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not attend any meetings where Joint Command was established. This document here says June 1998, and my opinion is that this is not correct, that what is written here is not correct; that is my personal opinion, based on what was done later on in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, you see it also says that the work was terminated in late 1998, the work of the Joint Command. Is that your understanding or could you commend on that?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have said, this document is totally new to me. And in my view, what is described here is not true, does not correspond to the truth of what was happening in Kosovo during these anti-terrorist activities. In my view, there was no Joint Command, not at all. Now, who wrote this here and for what reasons, I couldn't speculate. I know that no Joint Command existed down there nor am I familiar with any activities of that Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So you would not be able to tell us whether or not the Joint Command did in fact continue to operate in 1999?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It didn't operate in 1998 either. Now, do you really wish me to speculate about this? I can tell you what we did at the meetings and what co-ordination work we conducted in situations where I attended meetings and so on. Now, as to Joint Command, how it was established, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Mr. Djordjevic answered Mr. Stamp's questions three times before Mr. Stamp, in his following question, drew a totally opposite conclusion. I don't think that that's permissible. If the accused said three times that the Joint Command did not exist and that he didn't know about this document from 1998 and he believed it to be untrue, then how could the next question be formulated claiming that the Joint Command existed and that it existed in 1998 and so on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't read the passage of questions the way you do, Mr. Djurdjic. I don't think there's any basis for interfering with the cross-examination at the moment. Carry on, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You have referred us to the meetings and what you did at the meetings. Perhaps we could look at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: With the leave of the Court could the witness be handed a copy in B/C/S of P886, that is the notes of the meeting of the Joint Command, because we'll be moving from place to place in that document and it might be more convenient if he had a copy. May I, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. Can we look at P -- sorry, page 140 to 142 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And, Mr. Djordjevic, for you this is the meeting of the 28th of October. Let's look at page 140 in English first. Just to orient ourselves, you see that this -- at this meeting Mr. Minic opened the meeting. And can you make out from your copy that you were present at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not attend the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Are you on the 28th of October?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I concluded my activities in Kosovo on the 5th or 6th October, 1998, when the implementation of the global plan was completed. And from that point on I had nothing to do with any activities in Kosovo and Metohija, nor was I present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we scroll down to the bottom of page 140 on the English version, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If you look on your version in B/C/S, Mr. Djordjevic, do you see that after Mr. Gajic speaks you are recorded to have spoken?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I wasn't there then.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you see a reference to you speaking?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it says "Gen Djordjevic" here. Can we -- I can't read this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It records you saying here: "Following the pull-out of police units, I believe they will become more self-disciplined and behave more correctly." You were speaking about the implementation of the October Agreements, which required police units to withdraw -- some police units to withdraw. And if you continue on, Mr. Djordjevic, you'll see that General Lukic spoke after that and then you spoke again according to these minutes. And this is page 141 now in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we move on to page --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't remember attending this meeting. I know that after the signing of the agreement, pursuant to the order of the minister, General Stevanovic went to Kosovo and he informed of the obligations that police units had in relation to the agreement, but I really do not remember this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the second entry you are quoted as being suggesting -- or asking: "Can we submit information about the DTS," I think that's an acronym for the terrorist, "attacks on members of the MUP and the VJ to Mr. Sean of the CSCE," I think that should be Mr. Shaun Byrnes of the OSCE. Can you remember ever expressing a view that the attacks that were continuing in October should be submitted or information on the attacks should be submitted to Mr. Byrnes?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I really don't remember this meeting at all. As I've said, my involvement in Kosovo ended once the global plan was implemented, and from that time on I did not take part in any of the meetings, in particular meetings of this kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you go to October in -- did you go to Kosovo at all in October?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the second half of October I took part in the signing of the agreements. I also had some family problems. My father had died. And I really cannot recall having been there or -- in fact, I didn't have any other obligations, or I did not receive any orders from the minister to go down there and to do anything. So it's really completely unclear to me. The first time that I went back down there was when President Milutinovic was there, and then on the 15th of January, and then in 1999. That was the first time that I went back there. I don't remember this meeting at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. If we look at page 142 in English and for your copy it's the last entry for that day, the 28th of October. Mr. Minic said that you should have a thorough discussion on how to work with the OSCE or the CSCE. And in the next sentence he goes on to say: "I think that this command should remain unchanged and work until the end of the year, meeting when necessary." Wasn't Mr. Minic referring to the Joint Command, the command that existed which -- involving the meeting of the senior members of the MUP and the politicians, including yourself?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, who thought what, who said what, I can't really say that myself. Quite a lot of people spoke here, people who used that term, people who used it in their communication with other people. But I, as far as any participation is concerned, I can't recall this meeting. The next time when I was in Kosovo was when President Milutinovic was there. I accompanied him. And then I went back to Kosovo on the 15th of January when the Serbian prime minister visited Kosovo, and there were two or three other meetings down there during the war. And that sums up -- this is the sum total of my visits to Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Generally speaking during the course of 1998 when you attended these meetings, weren't -- wasn't it Mr. Minic or, if he wasn't there, Mr. Sainovic who led the meetings, who was the leader of this group of participants in these meetings?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not a group of participants. We have representatives of the army, of the police, and some politicians who had some tasks down there, who got together. Those meetings were usually opened by politicians. They would present opening remarks. That's how it was usually done. And then everybody would deal with issues in their line of work. They would brief the other participants about the most salient facts, and that's how it was done. The politicians, the military men, and the policemen would all inform the other participants about their line of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think you would agree with me that Mr. Minic and Mr. Sainovic were the most senior persons from the state governing apparatus of Serbia and the FRY who attended those meetings?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the highest-ranking persons as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we look at the document you have, that's the minutes, if you look at the first meeting - and this is page 2 in English, you see the participants?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Opened by the Assembly president, Mr. Minic. And after various persons had made their contributions, if you could look at the end of the notes for that day. And in English this is page 4. You see what is described here as conclusions of Mr. Minic, and he says, among other things: "Training must continue. "Carry out inspections." And that was the normal format of the meetings of -- of high-level administrative bodies in Serbia. I think you mentioned that was the format of the MUP collegium minutes -- MUP collegium meetings. You met, everybody said what they had to say, and the leader at the end would give his conclusions, in which he would give out instructions. Isn't it the same thing Mr. Minic is doing in giving the conclusions? He's giving instructions based on what he heard at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course not. Minic listened to what all the participants in the meeting had to say, and then he presented his own view. And I can say with full certainty that Minic could not have issued any orders to the police forces in Kosovo. And from all the documents, we have been able to see that all the orders that pertain to the drafting of documents were done by the Pristina Corps commander on the orders of his superior command, that's the 3rd Army command; and it says here in item 3 elaborating further tasks, General Pavkovic. Well, he's the one who actually kept the notes. That was his impression of what was going on. For me, the most important thing is that at this meeting Pavkovic says that the following action should be carried out in accordance with the general plan, and in order to prepare those documents he informed the police structures as to what axes would be done in the days that followed and what the MUP staff for the prevention of terrorism could see on the basis of this plan in terms of what forces would be needed for the involvement. And through its representative in the planning process, he would give his input for the drafting of the plans. And that's how it was done. The order to carry out tasks contained in the general plan were done by the Pristina Corps, with the input from the MUP staff for the prevention of terrorism. So the MUP staff had its own institutions, so to speak, that functioned 24 hours a day. The Pristina Corps had its command and its superior commands that were also working around-the-clock. So this meeting here took one hour, one hour, 15, one hour, 45 - the meetings of this kind took that long more or less - and after that the people would go back to their jobs. And then the next day or a couple of days later we would again all gather together, we would exchange information and so on and so forth. So everybody had their own command and at those meetings we simply exchanged information --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, much of what you just said, again you have said it before. I didn't ask you for this information. I'm trying to move through quickly. Just, please, focus on what I ask and give direct answers which -- and on that can I move on to another and ask you to just focus on the question. If we look at page 15 of this document in English. For you, sir, it's the meeting of the 27th of July, 1998. You see Mr. Minic, who is the Assembly president, says to: "Continue the plan at 0700 hours as agreed." Do you have it there? Yes. And if we look at another example of the 10th of September, 1998, that's at page 84 in English. If you could find the 10th of September, 1998. You see Mr. Minic is reported here to be saying: "Go into Dubrovnik and Radovic villages and see what the situation is like ... "Go into Papracani village and have the police occupy it." There's a VJ to do that and have the police occupy it. Later on: "Go into all villages and pressure them into handing over weapons. "Secure the road and control the territory. "The army will adopt a plan on arrangement of the territory on Monday. "The MUP should do the same ..." And this document is replete with situations like that. Look at it and look at the statements by the other participants at this meeting, and you will see the language here is in the nature of reporting. They are reporting and he is commanding. Can you see that, that on the face of this document ...

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, according to what it says there, I wasn't there. But regardless of whether I was present or not, I in general terms said what should be done and how. So Minic and other politicians just listened to the reports from other people, and they heard what the Pristina Corps had planned and what the Pristina Corps and the MUP staff had actually implemented. So he listened to that and he simply repeated what had been done in terms of concerted action by the police and the army or what they had planned to do on that day. So the Pristina Corps and the MUP forces did not wait for this order by Minic. It was not an order at all. I don't know. The army and the police forces did not wait for him to issue an order before they launched an action. They had an obligation to work in accordance with the general plan and with the documents drafted by the Pristina Corps. And they simply reported as to how far they had gone in terms of the implementation so that the army forces and the MUP staff and the Pristina Corps command would be kept fully briefed in the course of the implementation of the tasks in here. I don't consider this to be an order. If he had not ordered this to the army and to the police, that would mean that the army and the police would not do that; and quite the contrary was true. They had their own plans, their own orders, and they acted in accordance with that. This was just an exchange of information. At those meetings I never saw any maps or plans that were debated --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, yes --

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and then that some decisions were made. This was not done.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think you told us before that the maps and the planning at the operational level was done by the Pristina Corps. But what I'm suggesting to you is that it was done on the basis of the Joint Command decisions led by Mr. Minic and Mr. Sainovic. May I give you a couple of examples but this time with Mr. Sainovic. If you look at page 108 in the English copy, it's the 22nd of September. Now, of course Mr. Sainovic, if you look at that, you could see that he listened to everybody including yourself. And he says, among other things - this is his first comment at this meeting of the 22nd of September - and at the bottom of the page in English he says. "Regroup forces (transfer two PJP companies). "Continue the operation tomorrow." If we go to page 109 in English, and Mr. Djordjevic, it's the next entry or the next record of Mr. Sainovic speaking, he says: "When the operation ends, we must then engage the intervention unit to surround the village where the terrorists are." These sound to be instructions given on the basis of what has been said to him by the police and military leadership, Mr. Djordjevic. Why would Mr. Sainovic, who is the vice prime minister or the vice president of the FRY, be making these statements or issuing these directions in respect to police and military activity?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My response is the same as the one that regards Minic. His thoughts or his initiatives or his proposals as far as the army and the staff MUP are concerned were not tantamount to orders. The army and the police received orders from others, not from Sainovic, Zoran Andjelkovic, or Minic, who were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think you said Mr. Sainovic had responsibility for foreign affairs. Is that your recollection?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never said he was responsible for foreign affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know what his --

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sainovic was responsible for communication with the foreign representatives in Kosovo, and he was also the chairman of the Federal Commission for Co-operation with the OSCE.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So his role at these meetings, I think, what he could offer, if those were his sole functions down in Kosovo was briefings and what was transpiring in his contacts with these representatives of foreign organisations, not so?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, all of those politicians who were down there had their specific purviews. Minister Matkovic was in charge of the economic situation in Kosovo; that was his sphere of responsibility. Milomir Minic primarily dealt with the social and political structures in Kosovo. Sainovic was primarily obliged to deal with the international structures down there, to communicate with them. And Zoran Andjelkovic, as the president of the Provisional Executive Council in Kosovo and Metohija, was more concerned with the general issues of public administration in that area, in Kosovo. So they were not commanders. They did not exercise command over the army or the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, if you could go to the meeting on the 26th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And this is English at page 112.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Similarly, you see the military represented by General Pavkovic. If you read it you'll see it is basically in the nature of reporting. General Lukic then speaks, and it is generally telling about what happened in the past. Both of them are usually speaking in the past tense. You see then Mr. Sainovic closes the meeting, and he uses -- he's recorded as speaking about what you should do, he who is supposedly responsible for communication with overseas representatives, speaks to the leadership of the police and the army in this way. Wasn't it Mr. Milosevic who authorised him and Mr. Minic to speak to the leadership of the police and the army in that way, to give them instructions?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that order. I don't know whether Milosevic ordered anything to them. I know about the obligations that the staff had down there, the obligations related to anti-terrorist activities, and the politicians who were present there were entitled to comment on what the people attending the meeting briefed each other, what the representatives of the army and the police said to each other by way of exchanging information. Other than that, they did their job in accordance with the plans and not in accordance with any orders that Sainovic or Minic or anybody else might have issued to them. They could comment. They could say that perhaps something should be done differently in their line of work, but they were not issuing orders, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, you will agree with me here at least that Mr. Sainovic here was not speaking about anything in his line of work, foreign affairs?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's possible that there were no activities within his sphere of activity, so that's how it was -- so he talked about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: During the period when the five-stage plan was being implemented, would you -- or how frequently did you attend these meetings?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was in Pristina, I usually attended those meetings. I didn't attend them when I was absent, but as a general rule I was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If you could look at the meeting of the 12th of August, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is page 41 in English or in English the meeting begins at page 39, but if we could just move straight to page 41.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, what date are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The 12th of August, 1998. General Pavkovic -- I think since it's a fairly long meeting I should tell you there, it's the second time that General Pavkovic intervenes. He speaks about -- he speaks that operations should continue at Slup, Voksa, and Dulje. And you also intervened to say to: "Do Voksa and Slup and engage the army." And Mr. Minic, as he's warned to do, closed the meeting by saying: "Proceed further with the process on these three points: Slup, Voksa, and Lodja and prepare them." Do you recall this meeting? That can be answered yes or no.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right now after so many years, I naturally do not remember this meeting. I remember that there were activities in this area, but now to ask me to remember that the meeting was held on the 12th and that somebody drew conclusions and wrote down something, I really couldn't do that. I could just give you comments on what I had read here --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, you have answered my question --

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I suppose that the meeting was held --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could look at the next day, the 13th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: English page 44 [sic].

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You will see Mr. Pavkovic. Maybe I could help you if you can't find it. I think this is the second intervention by Mr. Pavkovic, near the end before Mr. Minic gives his conclusions. Mr. Pavkovic said that the Slup and Voksa action would begin with the 8th Detachment and that the Chief of Staff will lead the action in accordance with the -- well, let's say the suggestion by Mr. Minic in the previous meeting. I just want to point that out to you and ask you if you recall that.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here at the top it says that I wasn't present that day, and also what is quite typical is that Mr. Stanisic was present, he was there for a couple of days --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, never mind, never mind.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and he would always come to these meetings where he had things to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We're not interested in Mr. Stanisic. Mr. Stanisic is not the issue. It's your presence and you're quite correct. So we have traced the development of that operation. I'd like now first to look at P1232. You see that this is an order from the Pristina Corps command dated the 14th of August, 1998. You see that?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do. Actually, this is the first time that I see a decision of this sort. I have never seen anything like this up till now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In your preparations for your defence, and even in the course of this trial, you haven't seen any Pristina Corps order like this? Is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I want to say is that I saw for the first time decisions of this kind here --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- during preparations, after my arrival in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. This decision is on breaking up the terrorist forces in Slup and Voksa. And if we could move to the -- to page 3 in English, which is the last page in B/C/S -- well, let's move to page 4 in English first. You see it's signed by Chief of Staff, Colonel Lazarevic, as he then was. Last page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if we could remain there in B/C/S but go to the previous page in English -- no, no, remain there in B/C/S but go to the previous page in English. So please -- thank you. Thank you very much. And we are looking at item 6 at the bottom, and can you also look at item 6. The order that: "Combat operations will be commanded by the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija with the PrK forward command post in Djakovica." Isn't that how the system worked? I think you said earlier that plans would be drafted by the Pristina Corps professional staff and issued to the various people, the various units, that would participate?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At this period of time, in August, Chief of Staff of the Pristina Corps was Colonel Lazarevic, who was at that time permanently stationed at the forward command post of the Pristina Corps in Djakovica. He did not come to Pristina -- at least I didn't see him there. He was in Djakovica the entire time at the forward command post, and his main activities had to do with the protection of the border. These villages and these areas described here are close to the border. Now, as to why he formulated it in this way here, I really couldn't tell. I don't know what he means when he says that the combat operations will be commanded by the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija with the Pristina Corps forward command post in Djakovica. He was the Chief of Staff of the Pristina Corps at the forward command post in Djakovica, and I wasn't there with him in order to know how this text written in this document was implemented in practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let us go back to the first page. Just to be sure, the item 1 orders that the combat group is to be engaged to support the MUP forces in breaking up the enemy forces in Slup and Voksa villages. You were area that this operation that you discussed at the Joint Command meeting would involve MUP forces?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you that it wasn't a meeting of the Joint Command. It was our co-ordination --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well --

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and naturally Pavkovic briefed on this and I knew that both the forces of the army and the police would be engaged in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you see any type of order that was given or sent to MUP forces who would participate in this action?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not a single document. I personally didn't see a single document, either in relation to this action or any other action. I only saw a document pertaining to the first meeting and what was issued there collectively. I didn't see that commander of units received any order, and all of the documents went from the Pristina Corps to the staff; and then the staff would distribute them to whoever needed them. I personally never saw either this decision or any other decision of this type, nor the map that commanders normally received. Out in the field I only saw the maps of locations based on which they informed the staff about the whereabouts of individual units.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we have a look at document with 65 ter number 04487. And what is coming up is an attachment to this decision that is in front of you now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm trying to find this, this exhibit, in the list provided by the OTP and I can't find it. But never mind me, Ms. O'Leary can't find it either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can you assist, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I am told it's not on the list, but -- so I'll just move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, in your sojourn in Kosovo during these operations, you saw only one map that set out or described the disposition of MUP forces for these operations; is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw an encrypted map which unit commanders had, depicting locations in figures. The staff of the MUP had the same map, as did commanders of military units and their commands within the corps. So those were the maps based on which unit commanders could report to the staff without referring to the name of a location, but rather just giving figures which were codes for locations. They would call the staff and say, "I am near village 42." That's the only map I saw, that's the encrypted map produced by the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, weren't you aware that for each order like the one we just looked at for operations, there was a specific map for that operation which accompanied the order?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have said to you, I knew that they received excerpts about activities that were to be conducted and that were depicted on the map. I'm not sure whether this document that we saw, order, the textual part of it was distributed at all. I know that for PJPs --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you just focus on -- Mr. -- simply, simply, were you aware that for each operation there were issued specific maps that delineated the disposition of forces, including MUP forces, for that specific operation? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good. That's a straight answer. Thank you. Now, you were in the field in this period for many of these operations. Were you not interested in seeing the instructions and the maps that governed how the MUP forces were to participate in these operations?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the commanders who were duty-bound to work pursuant to those maps. I myself was out in the field, and I didn't really like maps because it's not what I'm very knowledgeable about. I did not interfere in their work with maps. They had their own responsibilities. I was present there. They moved about pursuant to the orders given to them and pursuant to the maps distributed. They harmonised that with the members of the army, and there was no need for me to supervise whether they were moving in accordance with what was written in the maps or not. I wasn't really interested in those maps.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How about the written text, the excerpts, that accompanied these maps to the unit commanders, you weren't interested in reading these -- even one of them for all of these operations that you went out on?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was the task of the staff. They also participated in drafting these plans. They would send their representative, and then they were duty-bound to convey that to all the units that were under their command. That was their responsibility. I was outside of that process of handing down orders and what was contained in documents and maps. I really don't know whether there were any written orders. I know that they received excerpts on the maps. Now, as to what was actually inside, to tell you the truth, I don't know; I never looked into any of those envelopes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In July, August, September, early October -- well, you have told us you were in the field most of the times. But about how many operations did you oversee or did you monitor?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really couldn't tell you, couldn't give you any figures now. I spent most of the time out in the field when these actions were conducted, so I couldn't give you any figures. Now, there were broader operations there covering several areas. I dealt with one axis and one area; other people dealt with others. So it wasn't possible for me to oversee all of that. Instead, I would mostly focus on the areas that were considered to be most problematic or expected to be. That's where I was. So if we look at the total number of those operations, I perhaps was there in one-third of them because there were really many of them in our area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we look again at P886, at the minutes of the meeting. And we want to get to page 24 in English. I think it's page 27. Can we have a look at page 27 in English. It's a meeting for the 1st of August, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you are speaking here that preparations for the -- tomorrow's operation have been completed, and that is in respect to the launching of the third phase of the plan. Do you recall that meeting?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a meeting. Now, as to whether I remember it, there was a meeting, I was present, and they recorded here what I had allegedly said. This was recorded by the person who took down the minutes. We don't know how it was done. My intervention here deals exclusively with the implementation of the plan that had been previously drafted by the Pristina Corps. I here speak of the direction that needs to be taken, and this is the sense of my words here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, I probably should advise that a document I referred to earlier by its 65 ter number, 01434, had been received in evidence as P1424 in -- 1422, P1422. I just state that for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we look at D312 -- sorry, D324. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You see General Pavkovic here is requesting of the 3rd Army commander approval to continue operations according to the above plan, that's in the last sentence of the document. But in the first sentence he notes that: "It was decided at a meeting of the Joint Command ... held on the 31st of July, 1998 ... to launch the third stage of the plan on the 2nd of August ..." Can you -- or may I just put it this way: Does this not remind you now that the combat plans, the combat orders that were prepared by the Pr, the Pristina Corps, were prepared on the basis of Joint Command orders?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know is that the commander of the Pristina Corps could not adopt any documents about implementing the general plan without previously receiving an order from his superior command. Now, as to what kind of communication he had with his command, what he wrote to them, and what they responded and what they ordered, I know nothing about that. All I know is that based on an order of some sort of a co-ordination body in Pristina, he was not authorised to move his units and carry out assignments. He could only receive assignments from his superior command, which was the command of the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And he -- you observe that he requests that approval on the basis of the decision of the Joint Command -- well, very well, that is something on the face of the document. I really should have shown you before the --

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know anything about their communication and correspondence, what they wrote to each other. I don't know that. I know that he would come in the evening to that meeting. He would inform us that he had just arrived from the meeting at the forward command post of his corps in Pristina. He would say, "We talked about this and that, I received such orders." Now, as to any further details, I really don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, if you look at the meeting of the 30th of July, that's a Joint Command meeting, the last -- and I think you have the minutes here. And this is at page 25 in the English.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: 30th of July, the last thing there is the execution of the third phase. General Pavkovic in the letter we were looking at earlier referred to a decision of the Joint Command of the 31st of July. I can tell you and you can see that that is not there on the 31st, but if you look for the previous day you will see part of the conclusions at the end of the meeting refers to exactly what you were saying, the execution of the third phase. You observe that? And --

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't. I can't find it in the documents here, but of course there was debate about the activities in the previous period and what was ahead in the days that followed. So this is nothing strange that was the methodology of work at those meetings. So people would be briefed, this stage was completed, or we have this stage ahead of us, or such and such a task has to be carried out which is in this stage. And on the basis of this discussion preparations are to be made, and those documents were then used as a basis for further action. So it is not controversial that security problems and security situation and anti-terrorist activities were discussed at those meetings, inter alia. Each of those politicians addressed problems that concerned him, but as Djakovic told us, he wrote down what was of interest to him. He didn't write down everything that was said and everything that was discussed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was wondering if it's a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have the first break now, to resume at 4.20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. If we could move on and have a look at P890.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is a decision by General Pavkovic, then commander of the Pristina Corps, on the joint engagement of MUP and VJ forces in -- if we look in paragraph 1 in various areas including Glodjane village, Prilep village sector. You are aware of this operation, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, I remember when you testified you spoke -- you were shown a video -- well, we'll get to that later. And if you could go down, if you could go to page 2 -- or let's scroll down in the B/C/S and stay on the same page in the English. And I think we'll have to go to the top of the next page in the B/C/S, please. You'll see, among other things, at 2.3.1 the reference - which is at the bottom of the page in English - to sending the 1st Motorised Battalion to Glodjane village. You see that?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could move to page 3 in the English, which is the last page I think in B/C/S. The bottom of page 6 in the English, command and control, that's item 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: General Pavkovic says, as you have seen before, that the: "Combat operations will be commanded by the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija ..." Now, you say that you never saw any of these orders in that time, neither did you see any of the excerpts that were given to the MUP units that were involved. But were you aware that at least in military circles they were referring to the command of these operations as being under the Joint Command? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's absolutely not correct, what you're saying now. This statement that the exercise of command over combat was carried out by the Joint Command from the forward command post of the Pristina Corps in Djakovica -- well, that's something that I am completely unaware of. I don't know what Joint Command. If we now take as a starting point that the Joint Command was Sainovic, Minic, Matkovic, and all those people who were down there, and if that means that they went to Djakovica, to the forward command post, to exercise command from there, well, that's not what happened. That's not how it was done. Civilians were never at command posts, they never exercised command. That was the first time that I saw Colonel Lazarevic - he was a colonel then - since he was the only person at the forward command post of the Pristina Corps as the Chief of Staff of the staff in Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When was the first time you heard the expression "Joint Command" used in reference to the operations that began in June/July 1998 in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when. It was the usual term that was used widely in the military circles by them, but if we look at the 22nd of July, the first meeting that was held, the person taking the notes says attending: Milomir Minic, the president of the Assembly, it's not correct. He was the president of the committee in the Yugoslav Assembly -- well, Sainovic, that's correct; Zoran Andjelkovic, minister; Djordjevic Rodoljub, deputy MUP, well --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, Mr. Djordjevic, please, please. I'm not saying that what you're saying is not interesting. I just want to know when it is, if you can recall approximately, you heard the expression "Joint Command" used in respect to the command or management structures that were in place for Kosovo in this operation in 1998?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm now telling you the first meeting that we held, nobody stood up, Minic, Sainovic, or anyone else to say: This is the Joint Command, I am the commander, this is my deputy, these are the members. This did not happen, and it never had that form. And then days later in the course of the communication, the term "Joint Command" was used. To my mind it was used to label this kind of a meeting where we exchanged information. But if you say a command, it has to have its elements: The commander. It has to have a permanent structure. Well, if --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. You said days later - and that is your answer - days later in the course of communication the term was used. When you first heard this term being used, what sort of communication, was it oral or written?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was no communique. It was just in regular conversation. It was not official. That term was just used as jargon, but it was primarily used by the military. And Djakovic explained that he coined the term even before all that was done down there in Kosovo. But to my mind, those meetings did not have any features that would mark it as a command of any sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could move on and have a look at P1422. This is another order issued by the Pristina Corps for operations in the Djakovica sector dated the 19th of September, 1998. And if we could look at page --

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not Djakovica, Cicavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, my pronunciation is really bad. That's what I meant. Sorry about that. Cicavica. If we look at page 5, please, in the English which is in Serbian page 3. At the task of the neighbouring units he describes what the MUP forces, what axes or what the forces would be doing. Just have a read of that and tell me if you recall this operation.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item 4, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. Items 3 and the first sentence of item 4.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Item 3 says that elements of the MUP forces in the Likovac-Poljance-Srednja Klina road -- Mitrovica road, Ovcarevo, Komorane, up to Belacevac, throw a wide cordon around the territory and control it to prevent an influx or spillover of the sabotage and terrorist forces from the combat sectors --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, do you remember this order -- sorry, do you remember this particular operation that is being referred to here?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you see in the second paragraph of item 3 he says: "Part of the Serbian population in the Serbian settlements shall cut off the right bank of the Sitnica river to prevent the DTS from crossing ..." And you see in the second sentence of item 4: "Engaging territorially based MUP forces and the Serbian population, throw a wide cordon around ... Cicavica ..." You were aware, Mr. Djordjevic, at that time that the -- there were armed members of the ethnic Serb population that was being used to supplement the MUP and the VJ forces in these operations?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were you aware that just about the time when this five-phase plan began there was a programme to arm members of the ethnic Serb population in the villages in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the question is imprecise. When the plan or the programme were adopted -- what kind of programme for civilians are you talking about if you're asking me if I knew about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know about any plan or policy of arming ethnic Serbs in the middle of 1998 in Kosovo, that's ethnic Serb civilians?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that at that time, after the operations started, in some ethnically Serb villages reserve police squads were set up and people who were members of those squads were issued some weapons. Now, as to any details of arming the Serb population in more general terms, I couldn't really tell you that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well --

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- but I think at any rate --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just to remind you, you recall that this operation that we're discussing was also discussed at Joint Command meetings. If you look at the meeting for the 19th of September, 1998, in the document you have.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is P886, if we could go to 103, page 103.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And it's also in your document, you could probably find it if you want to, the 19th of September, the entry for the 19th of September. And General Lazarevic is referring to the plan for Cicavica. That is the first person who spoke. You still maintain, Mr. Djordjevic, that you are not aware that in this action as well as in other actions armed Serb -- armed ethnic Serb civilians were used to supplement the MUP and the VJ forces?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a force acting in co-ordination with the army and the police in the implementation of some plans, they were not used. If there were any armed ethnic Serbs, civilians, if operations were carried out in an area, their only obligation was to protect their own village and they were not part of any attacks or offensive operations. But whoever wrote the plan included this category too. But based on my presence in the field, armed villagers never joined the police or the army forces to act jointly, to take part with them in anti-terrorist activities, never ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. So I take it that in respect to the order I just showed you, you are aware of the operation but you don't know about the part of the order that says that the Serbian population shall cut off the right bank of the river and shall participate with MUP forces in throwing a cordon, you don't know about that?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that action I was on the other side of the mountain. Since there was a mountain there, I was on the other side so I don't know. I didn't see then -- or actually in any other operation where I was present that the armed civilians were used to reinforce the army and the police. In 1998 there was no need for that, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In other words, you cannot -- you have no explanation as to why General Pavkovic would include that in this order?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why he put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Can we move on to look at P11 -- sorry, P1229. This, without going over to the next page, is signed by Lieutenant-General Pavkovic, commander of the Pristina Corps as he then was. He speaks here, first line, item 1 of a meeting in Belgrade on the 31st of August, 1998, presided over by the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. I think, but perhaps I'm mistaken, you mentioned that you were at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Along with -- from the MUP, that is, General Lukic, General Stevanovic, and the minister?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. According to the order of the President of Serbia, Milutinovic; Vlajko Stojiljkovic, the minister; myself; Generals Obrad Stevanovic and Lukic; and state security chief, were -- we were all there. And at that meeting, the Pristina Corps commander briefed those present on the involvement of the units of his corps and the army in the implementation of the plan so far. The head of the MUP staff for the prevention of terrorism, General Sreten Lukic, briefed the meeting about the participation of the police units. And then General Pavkovic presented the plan for the implementation of the fifth stage in the plan to prevent terrorism. So that's how it was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if we look at page 2 in the English, item 4, I think it is also page 2 in the B/C/S but perhaps we could scroll down first to see if it's on the first page of the B/C/S. Well, it begins, you could read those three lines and then we could move to the next page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which item? Is it item 4?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: 4, 4, please.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please put back the first page. At a meeting of the ZK for Kosovo and Metohija on 10 September, I repeated that request and proposed the following --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I don't know what he's writing about here, it's really not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, do you remember -- well, firstly doesn't ZK, what you see there, doesn't that refer in Serbian to the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Based on this letter, yes, this could stand for Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And he's saying that during a briefing of the Joint Command it was pointed out that a VJ had not formed rapid intervention helicopter units as the SRJ president had ordered at the meeting of the 31st of August, 1998. Do you recall at that meeting with the president, on the 31st of August, 1998, there was discussion and an order that there should be rapid intervention helicopter units?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that that topic was included in the discussion -- I think that at a meeting with President Milosevic as well, but I cannot be certain at this time. I know that it was envisaged that in order to proceed as efficiently as possible there should be a team established which would use the helicopters of the Army of Yugoslavia and that there should be also MUP members involved, but it's been too many years since then and I can't remember any details. I just know that there were some discussions concerning this. I cannot remember what duties the MUP staff had and what the Pristina Corps was supposed to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you recall it being discussed at the meetings of the body referred to as the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it was discussed there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Let's look at -- have a look at that -- but before we do, if you look at the next page, just at the bottom there, the last paragraph you see before "we propose." You see that General Pavkovic, having complained that everything had not been done by the 3rd Army command in respect of delivering these -- these rapid intervention helicopter units, he says: "We are giving the members of the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija the opportunity to report to the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia that the VJ has not carried out its duties under the plan." Isn't General Pavkovic here saying that the Joint Command could report to the VJ, to the supreme commander, the president, for failing to carry out its decisions?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He says there: "We are giving the members of the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija the opportunity to report to the president of the FRY that the Army of Yugoslavia has not carried out its duties under the plan." Once again, this is the command of the Pristina Corps communicating with the army commander and other members that he mentions here, and again this is his vision of the matters. The MUP staff did not have such problems and it did not address anyone on this issue. Now, as to what were his motives in writing this, I really wouldn't be able to tell you. I know that there were problems of organising this unit and that ultimately it wasn't organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yeah, but in Serbian -- when you read the Serbian, he's effectively saying that the Joint Command could report to the VJ, to the supreme commander, President Milosevic; isn't that what it's saying?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. That's what it says there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if we could look briefly at the P886, that's the minutes of the meeting, at -- for the 11th of September, I think, 87 -- oh, I think you're absent from this meeting, Mr. Djordjevic, but you could still go ahead to find the meeting of the 11th of September. You see that General Pavkovic -- I'm sorry, I have I think the wrong reference here. Thank you. It's not here. Pardon me, I think we will have to return to that reference once it's found. But you recall that the rapid intervention units were decided upon or discussed at least at Joint Command -- meetings of this body that is sometimes referred to as the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. You're completely right. It was discussed, but no decision was made nor could it have been made. At that meeting and at those various gatherings where we tried to agree, we could only give proposals. And this is one such case. However, the request and the proposals of these people here - and I think they are from the 3rd Army or perhaps from the army in general - this never materialised. They never ultimately came out with these proposals nor could it have been done by what you call Joint Command. So nobody ultimately gave those helicopters because they would have needed an order for that, they would have needed to establish that unit, and to send those helicopters into combat assignments. It wasn't done because these people here did not really have any Joint Command with all the power that normally goes along with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could move on to another part of that -- this record, and this is page 140 I think in the copy you have, but it is the meeting - and I'm moving on to a slightly different topic. It is the -- it is page 140 in the English. Meeting of the 28th of October --

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you please give me the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: 28th October. You had indicated before that you can't recall being present at this meeting, and I had shown you two passages where you're recorded to have spoken.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we scroll down to the bottom there and then move on to the next page in English where General Djordjevic speaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It says there that you asked if you could submit information about the terrorist attacks on members of the MUP and the VJ to Mr., obviously, Shaun Byrnes of the OSCE. And finally if we could look at the last page in English, the end of the meeting. I think I had shown you where Mr. Minic referred to continuation of the command. He said the command should remain unchanged, but what I want to focus on is the person who spoke before that, General Pavkovic, who, in the English, said: "We must bear in mind the use of armed people and how to include them in defending roads." Can you recall participating in any of these meetings where the use of armed people was discussed? And that is the use of armed people by the MUP and the VJ.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm -- apologise. I wish to say just one sentence. The last meeting I attended was on the 6th of October. After the 6th of October until the 28th of October you cannot see me attending any of the meetings of this body called the Joint Command, and then after 22 days I show up at this meeting as shown here in the minutes. So the situation --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So, Mr. Djordjevic --

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- is completely unclear to me. I do not remember that these meetings Pavkovic briefed on the use of civilians in order to protect roads. I simply do not remember that. At that time, in my view, there was absolutely no reason to engage some armed Serb civilians. So that is not clear to me at all. It is clear to me when we are discussing reserve police squads or some other units, I know what we're talking about, what their duties were, and so on. But this here, I really cannot comprehend it. It's been a long time and I am sure that armed Serb civilians were not used in anti-terrorist activities as a force that acted in co-ordination with the army and the police. Now, who recorded what here, who uttered what, I really don't know how to comment on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You see in the document, you just mentioned that, that it records quite clearly when you're absent for a long stretch of meetings. It also records quite clearly when you're present. You see that?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we look at P1221.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The last entry from the Joint Command -- from the minutes of Joint Command that we were looking at refer to you as saying that -- as asking if you could submit information about the DTS attacks on members of the MUP and the VJ to Mr. Byrnes, and I want you to bear that in mind as you look at this document. This is an operations report of the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija dated the 28th of October, 1998, and it gives information on a variety of issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could move to page 2 in the English, also page 2 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You see it refers to "terrorist actions." Under item II, Roman numeral II, (b) "against the MUP. 1, in Retimlje village, Orahovac; 2, Gornja Klina village, Kosovska Mitrovica; 3," you can see that in the B/C/S copy "Komorane village on the Prizren-Djakovica road."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if we could move to page 3 in the English and page 3 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It continues to list the actions, the terrorist actions as it is put, against the MUP -- well, first, were you aware of these terrorist actions that is reported in this document?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How would I know that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are allegations here and most likely that's how it was. I wish to tell you this. I concluded my activities on the 5th of October --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- on the 5th of October I went to Belgrade. I worked as chief of public security there. I took part in negotiations with OSCE and NATO. I buried my father, and following that I returned. And then according to this I was there for just one day before going back to Belgrade. I don't know about this document that you're putting to me now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic --

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know under whose instruction it was written. I don't know to whom it was addressed, I know nothing of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- please answer my questions. Please. Were you aware -- were you aware of these --

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- terrorist actions, as they are reported here?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, you're asking me after ten years to recall a specific anti-terrorist -- or, rather, terrorist action. It says here that there was a terrorist activity on such and such day at such and such hour. I have no reason to doubt this, but neither did I know then nor do I know now that this terrorist activity was really conducted because I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That would be the short answer, and I'm going to ask you again: Please just focus on the questions and answer the questions that I ask you. Had you ever seen any report like this before, an operational report of the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You note that it is of the same date as when the Joint Command minutes, the minutes of the meeting of the Joint Command, record you as saying -- as asking whether or not you could report the KLA actions, the DTS attacks on members of the MUP and VJ to Mr. Byrnes? I'm suggesting to you, Mr. Djordjevic, that these attacks recorded in the minutes -- sorry, in the report here are the same attacks that you were referring to when you attended that Joint Command meeting.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not contentious that the staff knew about all of these events listed in the report. It is also not contentious that the staff informed Shaun Byrnes and KDOM about all of these terrorist activities; that has already been clarified here. But at that time I neither knew of this information -- I simply didn't have it because I was out of all of this for some 20 days. As I have told you, most likely all of this information contained here about these events is correct, but I simply don't know about this because I was completely out for about -- for a certain period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What do you mean by "completely out"?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not deal with these matters. I had no contact with these matters. I told you what my duties were between the 5th of October up until -- I don't know. It says here that I attended this meeting. I'm telling you that I spent 22 days in Belgrade discharging the duties that I have told you about earlier. As for these activities, the staff was informed about all of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let's look at P87. This is the next day, 29th of October, 1998. It's headed the "Minutes of the Meeting of the Operations Inter-Departmental Staff for the Suppression of Terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija 1998," held at Beli Dvor palace Belgrade, 29th of October, 1998, chaired by President Milosevic, and including you among the leadership figures present.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you remember that meeting?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could move to page 2 in English, let's start at the bottom of page 1 in B/C/S, so it should remain on the same page in B/C/S and go to page 2 in English. In the presence of all these dignitaries and leadership figures, including yourself, the minutes there record General Pavkovic as speaking on behalf of the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija. General Pavkovic went on to make a presentation. Do you remember that General Pavkovic spoke on behalf of the Joint Command at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Pavkovic spoke at the meetings held previously regarding these matters. He spoke about the forces of his corps. And when it comes to police forces that acted in co-ordination with the army, then it was General Sreten Lukic, head of the MUP staff, who briefed on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, who recorded these minutes and how this was drafted, I really wouldn't be able to tell you. I saw these minutes now for the first time during preparations for the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, the minutes were compiled - we don't need to go to the back of the document - by Lieutenant-General Slavoljub Susic, who was the chief of the cabinet for the Supreme Command of Yugoslavia. And he puts it here in his record that General Pavkovic spoke on behalf of the Joint Command. Do you recall - and this is a simple question, you could answer: Yes, I recall; no, I don't recall - do you recall that General Pavkovic did so, that he spoke on behalf of the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please. First of all, I don't know that I was a member of the operational staff for the prevention of terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija, inter-departmental staff, and I am unfamiliar with the term. And I did not attend meetings as member of the inter-departmental staff. Now, I don't know why the minute-taker used this name to label that meeting. I don't know that. It would be good --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic --

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- for that to be explained, how come that now we have this term.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
